usage: I have a reservation (just so you know)
Polite; said as you walk in to check in
반말, only telling a friend, never the staff
Formal 합쇼체, upscale salon or sounding crisp
I didn't book — is it possible (to walk in)?
The walk-in version when you have no booking
examples: 안녕하세요, 예약했는데요.
Hi, I have a reservation.
The standard check-in line said right after greeting; -는데요 softly invites them to look you up rather than just announcing a fact
세 시에 예약했는데요. 이름은 김민수예요.
I booked for three o'clock — the name is Kim Minsu.
Add time and name together so the receptionist can find your booking instantly
A: 어서 오세요. / B: 예약했는데요. 네이버로 했어요.
A: Welcome! / B: I have a reservation — I booked through Naver.
네이버 예약 is how the vast majority of Koreans reserve salons; mentioning it helps staff locate your booking in the right system
nuance: 예약했는데요 is 예약(을) 하다 ('to make a reservation', Sino-Korean 豫約) in the past tense plus the soft ender -는데요, meaning roughly 'I booked, so… (I'm here / please check)'. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it hands the situation over to the staff and invites them to look you up, rather than barking a flat statement. You use this in 존댓말 to salon staff the moment you arrive; with a close friend you'd drop to 예약했어, but 반말 is completely off-limits with any service worker. The nearest alternative is plain 예약했어요, which is grammatically fine but a shade more abrupt since it lacks that inviting soft ender. The classic English-speaker error is translating 'I have a reservation' with 있다: 예약이 있어요 is understandable but sounds like announcing an abstract fact rather than actively checking in — Koreans reach for the verb 하다 (예약했는데요). Another trap is the particle: it's 예약을 하다 (object), so never 예약에 했어요. In practice, most Korean salon bookings happen through Naver, so 네이버로 예약했는데요 is the single most common form you'll actually hear.

structuredNuance.t: 예약(을) 하다 is Sino-Korean 豫約 + 하다 ('make a reservation'). The past tense 예약했- plus soft ender -는데요 means roughly 'I booked, so…' — the -는데요 hands the moment to the staff and implicitly says 'please check me in', rather than stating a flat fact.
존댓말 to any service worker; said the instant you walk through the door. Drop to 예약했어 only with a friend you're telling — never to staff. Upscale salons may prefer the crisper 예약했습니다.
예약했어요 is the plain polite form — fine but a touch more abrupt. -는데요 softens further and invites a response, making it the more natural check-in phrase.
네이버로 예약했는데요 (booked via Naver), 카카오로 예약했는데요 (via Kakao), 세 시에 예약했는데요 (booked for 3 o'clock). Each adds the context staff need to locate your booking.

'I have a reservation' tempts learners to use 있다: 예약이 있어요 is grammatical but sounds like you're announcing a fact, not checking in. Use the verb 하다 (예약했는데요). Also watch the particle: 예약을 하다, never 예약에 했어요.

mistakes: Saying 예약이 있어요 to check in.
It's grammatical but means 'a reservation exists', which sounds detached. Koreans use the verb 하다: 예약했는데요 / 예약했어요 ('I made a booking').
Dropping -는데요 to a flat 예약했어요 and stopping there.
It works but is blunter and doesn't invite the staff to respond. -는데요 softens it and signals 'so please check me in': 예약했는데요.
Using 반말 예약했어 with the receptionist.
예약했어 is 반말, far too casual for staff you don't know. Keep 존댓말: 예약했는데요 or 예약했어요.

usage: Polite; declaring you only want a haircut, nothing else
반말, to a friend, not to the stylist
I would like just a cut
I'd like to get my hair cut
Softer way to open with what you came for
examples: 오늘은 커트만 할게요.
Today I'll just get a cut.
오늘은 ('today') frames it as a one-day choice, leaving the door open for other services another time
펌은 안 하고 커트만 할게요.
No perm — just a cut, please.
-만 ('only') paired with 안 하고 explicitly rules out add-ons the stylist might otherwise assume
A: 오늘 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 커트만 할게요. 얼마예요?
A: What can I do for you today? / B: Just a cut, please — how much is it?
Pair the declaration with 얼마예요 to confirm the price before you sit down
nuance: 커트만 할게요 is 커트 (the loanword 'cut') + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 form of 하다, announcing your intention politely). The particle -만 is doing the real work: it tells the stylist you want ONLY a haircut and nothing extra — no perm, no dye — which matters because salons often upsell or automatically include treatments. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the friendly customer register, polite but not stiff. Koreans write 커트 for a haircut (헤어컷 also appears on menus), and the plain verb for the action is 머리(를) 자르다 ('to cut hair') — the two are interchangeable, with 커트 sounding more salon-technical. The dividing line from 머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') is that 커트만 할게요 actively EXCLUDES other services via -만, while 자르려고요 simply states your purpose. The English-speaker trap is placing -만 in the wrong position: 커트 할게요만 is broken (만 attaches to the noun, not the sentence end), and substituting 그냥 ('just/casually') gives 그냥 커트 할게요 = 'I'll just casually get a cut' — a different nuance that doesn't exclude add-ons. Also note: for hair the loanword is 커트, not 컷 (컷 is for film editing).

structuredNuance.t: 커트 ('cut', loanword) + -만 ('only') + 할게요 (polite first-person intention). The particle -만 is the key: it signals you want ONLY a haircut, actively excluding perms, dye, and other add-ons the stylist might assume.
존댓말 to the stylist; the first thing you say after sitting down or when asked what service you want. 커트만 할게요 is warm and natural — not stiff, not overly casual.
머리 자르려고요 ('I came to get a cut') just states your purpose without the exclusion force of -만. Use 커트만 if you specifically want to head off upselling.
오늘은 커트만 할게요 ('just a cut today'), 커트만 하고 싶어요 ('I only want a cut'), 커트만 해 주세요 (slightly more of a request). All use -만 on 커트.

Two traps: (1) putting -만 at the end — 커트 할게요만 is wrong; 만 attaches to the noun: 커트만. (2) Using 그냥 to mean 'just a cut': 그냥 커트 할게요 means 'I'll just casually get a cut' — it doesn't exclude add-ons the way -만 does.

mistakes: Misplacing 만 as 커트 할게요만.
만 ('only') attaches to the noun, not the sentence end. Correct: 커트만 할게요.
Using 그냥 to mean 'just a cut'.
그냥 커트 할게요 means 'I'll just casually get a cut' (no strong reason). To mean 'only a cut, nothing else', use 만: 커트만 할게요.
Saying 머리 컷 주세요 like ordering an object.
A haircut isn't 'given' like a dish. Use the verb: 커트만 할게요 or 머리 좀 잘라 주세요.

english: Just tidy it up / trim it, please
usage: Polite; light cleanup, not a big change
반말, to a friend cutting your hair
Could you tidy it up, please?
끝만 살짝 ('only the tips, slightly') for a tiny trim
examples: 길이는 그대로, 다듬어만 주세요.
Keep the length — just tidy it up.
길이는 그대로 ('length as is') signals zero shortening; 다듬다 handles only the shape and damaged ends
끝이 좀 상했어요. 다듬어 주세요.
The ends are a bit damaged — please trim them.
상하다 ('to be damaged') gives the reason; the stylist now knows it's a maintenance trim, not a style change
A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 많이 자르지 말고 그냥 다듬어 주세요.
A: How would you like it done? / B: Don't cut much — just tidy it up.
많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') stacks before 다듬어 주세요 for extra protection against over-cutting
nuance: 다듬어 주세요 is 다듬다 ('to trim, neaten, tidy up') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form ('please do for me'). This is the single most useful salon word for someone who does NOT want a dramatic change: 다듬다 means cleaning up the shape and split ends while keeping essentially the same length and style. The crucial contrast is with 자르다 ('to cut'): 자르다 implies actually shortening and removing length, while 다듬다 implies maintenance — if you say 잘라 주세요 the stylist may take off far more than you wanted, so for 'just a trim' always reach for 다듬다. Stack intensifiers like 끝만 살짝 ('just the tips, lightly') or 많이 자르지 말고 ('without cutting much') to make the limit unmistakable. The English-speaker trap is exactly this verb choice: 'trim' maps mentally to 자르다, producing a real haircut when you wanted maintenance. Conjugation note: 다듬다 keeps the ㅁ intact — the form is 다듬어 주세요, never 다듬아 주세요 or 다듬워 주세요. Bare 다듬으세요 is also wrong for this context: it would command the stylist to trim their own hair rather than requesting they trim yours.

structuredNuance.t: 다듬다 literally means 'to make neat/tidy'. In the salon it specifically means a light cleanup — trimming split ends and restoring the shape without shortening the overall length. The -아/어 주세요 form makes it a polite favor request: 'please do this for me'.
존댓말 with all salon staff. Use when your hair is growing out of shape but you don't want length removed. Stack 끝만 살짝 or 길이는 그대로 to make the scope clear.
자르다 = cut (removes length); 다듬다 = tidy up (keeps length, shapes ends). These are the critical two verbs. If you say 잘라 주세요 when you meant 다듬어 주세요, you may come out with a noticeably shorter haircut.
끝만 살짝 다듬어 주세요 (only the very tips), 다듬어 주시겠어요? (more formal), 다듬어 줘 (반말). For the opposite — an actual cut — switch to 잘라 주세요.

'Trim' mentally maps to 자르다 for English speakers, but 자르다 means cutting and shortening. Always use 다듬다 for a light maintenance trim. Also: 다듬어 not 다듬아/다듬워 (the ㅁ is preserved, not subject to ㅏ/ㅗ vowel harmony).

mistakes: Saying 잘라 주세요 when you only want a trim.
자르다 ('cut') means shortening/removing length. For a light cleanup that keeps the length, use 다듬다: 다듬어 주세요.
Conjugating it as 다듬아 주세요 or 다듬워 주세요.
다듬다 is a regular verb keeping ㅁ: the form is 다듬어 주세요, not 다듬아/다듬워.
Saying 다듬으세요 to the stylist.
Bare 다듬으세요 is a command to the listener to trim (their own) hair. The favor form 다듬어 주세요 means 'please trim mine for me'.

english: Please don't make it too short
usage: Please don't make it too short
Polite; capping how short they go
반말, to a friend cutting it
Please don't make it too long
The opposite, when you want it shorter
examples: 앞은 괜찮은데 옆은 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
The front's fine, but don't make the sides too short.
Targeting one zone (옆 'sides') with the limit while leaving the rest alone
저번에 너무 짧게 잘라서, 이번엔 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
Last time it was cut too short, so this time please not too short.
저번에 … 잘라서 ('last time [they] cut it …, so') explains why you're being cautious this visit
A: 어느 정도 자를까요? / B: 귀는 덮을 정도로, 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요.
A: About how much shall I take off? / B: Long enough to cover my ears — not too short.
귀를 덮다 ('cover the ears') gives the stylist a concrete anchor length
nuance: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 is 너무 ('too') + 짧다 ('short') turned into the -지 않게 negative adverb form + 해 주세요 ('please make it'). The structure [-지 않게 해 주세요] = 'please make it so that it is NOT ~' is a powerful, reusable frame for setting limits on any salon service. Here it allows cutting while capping the result: 'cut, but don't go so far that it's too short'. The closest alternative 너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 uses the direct prohibitive -지 마세요 ('don't do X') — equally correct, but slightly more confrontational; the -지 않게 version describes the desired state rather than forbidding the action, so it sounds gentler and is preferred by most customers. The English-speaker trap is the double-negative word order: 너무 안 짧게 misplaces the negation (안 must go before the adjective inside the conjugated form, i.e. 짧지 않게, not 안 짧게 tacked in freely), and scrambled forms like 짧지 않게 너무 also break. A second trap: hair length is 짧다 ('short'), not 작다 ('small') — never say 너무 작지 않게. And 너무 skews negative ('excessively'), fitting perfectly here; don't swap it with 많이, since 많이 짧지 않게 sounds awkward.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 = 'please make it in a way that is not too short'. 너무 ('excessively') + 짧지 않게 ('-지 않게' negative adverb of 짧다) + 해 주세요. The -지 않게 해 주세요 frame sets a limit by describing the unwanted result state rather than banning the action.
존댓말 to staff. Said at the start of the cut or when the stylist asks how short to go. Especially useful if you've been over-cut before or if your hair grows slowly.

너무 짧게 자르지 마세요 (prohibitive -지 마세요) is equally correct but a touch more direct. The -지 않게 form is preferred in polite customer speech because it frames the desired result rather than issuing a prohibition.
너무 길지 않게 해 주세요 ('not too long'); 너무 짧지 않게만 해 주세요 (with 만 for emphasis); 조금만 자르고 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 ('cut just a little, not too short').
Two traps: (1) misplacing 안 — the negation belongs inside the conjugation as 짧지 않게, not freely placed as 너무 안 짧게; (2) using 작다 ('small') for hair length — hair is 짧다 ('short'), never 작다.

mistakes: Saying 너무 안 짧게 해 주세요.
The negation goes on the adjective with -지 않게: 짧지 않게. 너무 안 짧게 misplaces 안 and sounds broken.
Using 작다 instead of 짧다 for hair.
작다 means 'small in size'. Hair length is 짧다 ('short'). Say 너무 짧지 않게, not 너무 작지 않게.
Dropping 해 주세요 and saying just 너무 짧지 않게.
Without the verb it's an incomplete fragment. Finish it: 너무 짧지 않게 해 주세요 (or … 잘라 주세요).

english: Please give me bangs / keep the bangs down
usage: Polite; asking for front fringe forward over the forehead
반말, to a friend styling your hair
The opposite: 까다, swept off the forehead
Please trim my bangs a bit
Trimming the fringe specifically, not changing how it's worn
examples: 앞머리 있는 게 좋아서 내려 주세요.
I like having bangs, so please keep them down.
있는 게 좋다 ('prefer having') states the preference; the stylist now knows the fringe should come forward
앞머리 내려 주시고, 눈썹 정도 길이로 해 주세요.
Bangs down, please, and about eyebrow length.
눈썹 정도 길이 ('about eyebrow length') is the standard concrete cut-line for bangs in Korean salons
A: 앞머리는 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 원래 앞머리 까는데, 오늘은 한번 내려 볼까 해요.
A: What shall we do with the bangs? / B: I usually push them back, but today I'm thinking of trying them down.
까다 vs. 내리다 contrast in one exchange; -아 볼까 해요 ('thinking of trying') is a natural hedge
nuance: 앞머리 내려 주세요 is 앞머리 (lit. 'front-head', the fixed Korean word for bangs/fringe) + 내리다 ('to lower, bring down') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. 내리다 describes how you WEAR the fringe — down over the forehead. The essential opposite is 까다: 앞머리(를) 까다 means to push the fringe UP and BACK off the forehead — these two verbs produce completely different looks, so mixing them up at the salon chair is a real-world disaster. To MAKE bangs from scratch, say 앞머리 만들어 주세요; to TRIM existing bangs, say 앞머리 다듬어/잘라 주세요; to WEAR them down, 앞머리 내려 주세요. The English-speaker trap starts with vocabulary: there is no obvious Korean cognate for 'bangs', so learners describe it ('the hair in front') — just lock in 앞머리. A secondary trap is reaching for 자르다 thinking 'bangs = cut bangs', but 내리다 is purely about the wearing direction, not the cutting. Note that 머리 alone means 'head/hair' in general; the front fringe is specifically 앞머리. Keep 존댓말 with the stylist throughout.

structuredNuance.t: 앞머리 (lit. 'front-head', = bangs/fringe) + 내리다 ('lower/bring down') + 주세요. This isn't about cutting — it describes how the fringe is WORN: pulled forward and down over the forehead, as opposed to pushed back off it.

존댓말 to the stylist. Said during the style consultation, usually right after discussing the cut length. Works both when requesting new bangs and when telling the stylist how to finish styling the fringe you already have.
앞머리 까다 = push bangs UP/BACK (completely opposite look). 앞머리 만들어 주세요 = create bangs from scratch. 앞머리 다듬어 주세요 = trim existing bangs. Never swap 내리다 with 까다.
앞머리 내려 주시고, 눈썹 정도 길이로 해 주세요 (down + length cue). 앞머리 살짝만 내려 주세요 ('just slightly down'). 앞머리 옆으로 넘겨 주세요 ('sweep bangs to the side').

Two traps: (1) not knowing the word 앞머리 and describing 'the hair in front' instead — just learn 앞머리; (2) reaching for 자르다 ('cut') when you mean 내리다 ('wear down') — cutting and wearing direction are different requests.

mistakes: Confusing 내리다 with 까다.
앞머리 내리다 = wear bangs down over the forehead; 앞머리 까다 = push them back off the forehead. They're opposites — pick the right one.
Describing it as 앞에 있는 머리 instead of 앞머리.
Korean has a set word: 앞머리 ('bangs/fringe'). The roundabout 앞에 있는 머리 is unnatural and unclear to the stylist.
Using 자르다 when you mean to create or keep bangs.
To make bangs say 앞머리 만들어 주세요; to keep them worn down say 앞머리 내려 주세요. Plain 자르다 just means 'cut' and is ambiguous here.

english: Please make it like this photo
usage: Please make it like this photo
Polite; showing a reference picture to guide the entire style
Pointing or gesturing when you have no photo
Could it turn out like this photo?
Asking whether the look is achievable for your hair type
examples: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요. 가능해요?
Make it like this photo, please — is it possible?
Always follow with 가능해요? — reference photos show someone else's hair, which may not suit yours
이 사진처럼 하고 싶은데, 제 머리로 될까요?
I want it like this photo — would it work with my hair?
제 머리로 될까요 ('would it work with my hair') asks the stylist for a realistic professional opinion
A: 어떤 스타일 원하세요? / B: 이 사진처럼 자연스럽게 해 주세요.
A: What style do you want? / B: Natural, like this photo, please.
Adding 자연스럽게 ('naturally') guides the vibe even if the exact look can't be replicated
nuance: 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like, in the manner of') + 해 주세요 ('please do it for me'). Showing a reference photo is the single most reliable way to communicate a hairstyle across a language gap, and -처럼 is the particle that fuses directly onto the noun to express 'in the manner of': 사진처럼, never with a preceding object particle. A close alternative is 사진같이 (사진 + 같이), which is equally natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here, with -처럼 feeling a touch more standard in this context. The English-speaker trap is over-engineering the sentence: 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 ('make it LOOK like this photo') is understandable but wordier than what Koreans actually say — plain 이 사진처럼 해 주세요 is the natural form. A second pitfall is forgetting the realism check: the photo likely shows someone else's texture, thickness, or face shape, so Korean customers routinely add 가능해요? or 될까요? after handing over the phone. Keep 존댓말; the favor form 해 주세요 makes it a polite request, not a command.

structuredNuance.t: 이 사진 ('this photo') + -처럼 ('like/in the manner of') + 해 주세요. The particle -처럼 attaches directly to the noun — no gap, no object particle before it. The phrase means 'please execute the style you see in this photo'.
존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the very start of the consultation while holding out your phone. Almost always followed by 가능해요? or 될까요? to reality-check the look.
사진같이 해 주세요 is equally natural; -처럼 and 같이 are near-interchangeable here. 이렇게 해 주세요 ('do it like this') works when you're pointing but have no photo.
이 사진처럼 자연스럽게 해 주세요 (natural vibe); 이 사진이랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 ('similar to this photo', allowing differences); 이 사진처럼 될까요? (feasibility check).

Two traps: (1) adding a particle before 처럼 — 사진을 처럼 or 사진의 처럼 are both wrong; -처럼 fuses straight onto the noun; (2) over-building as 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 — this is understandable but unnatural; just say 이 사진처럼 해 주세요.

mistakes: Adding a particle before 처럼, like 사진을 처럼.
-처럼 attaches straight to the noun with no object particle: 사진처럼 해 주세요, not 사진을 처럼.
Saying 이 사진처럼 보이게 해 주세요 every time.
It's correct but wordy. Natives simply say 이 사진처럼 해 주세요; the 보이게 ('so it looks') is usually unnecessary.
Confusing 처럼 ('like/similar') with 때문에 ('because').
처럼 means 'in the manner of'. Don't swap in 때문에; 이 사진 때문에 해 주세요 would wrongly mean 'do it because of this photo'.

english: Please keep it similar to my hair now
usage: Keep it similar to my hair now
Polite; same style, just maintained — the go-to for a returning client
Keep it like it is now
그대로 ('as is') signals zero style change at all
똑같이 ('identically') for a precise repeat of a previous visit
examples: 크게 바꾸지 말고 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
Nothing drastic — keep it similar to my hair now.
크게 바꾸지 말고 ('without big changes') stacks with 비슷하게 to doubly signal you want maintenance, not reinvention
지금 머리랑 비슷하게, 길이만 좀 줄여 주세요.
Similar to now, just shorten the length a bit.
길이만 줄이다 ('only shorten the length') is the one permitted tweak — style stays, length adjusts
A: 오늘 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
A: How can I do it for you today? / B: Similar to what you did last time, please.
해 주신 거 ('what you did for me') references a past appointment, implying trust in the stylist's previous work
nuance: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 is 지금 머리 ('my hair now') + -랑 (colloquial 'with/and', the comparison linker) + 비슷하게 (adverb of 비슷하다 'to be similar') + 해 주세요. The pattern 'A랑 비슷하게 해 주세요' = 'please make it similar to A' is broadly reusable throughout the salon. The particle -랑 is the spoken, casual form; formal writing prefers -과/와, but -랑 is the natural choice in the salon chair. The critical three-way contrast: 비슷하게 allows minor differences and is best when small adjustments are fine; 똑같이 demands a precise repeat; 그대로 signals absolutely no change at all — choose based on how tightly you want the result controlled. The English-speaker trap is mixing the comparison frames: 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게 is redundant (처럼 'like' and 비슷하게 'similarly' say the same thing) — use one or the other. Also, 비슷하다 is an adjective, not a command verb; you cannot say 비슷하세요 to the stylist. You need the adverb form 비슷하게 paired with the action verb 해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 = 'please make it similar to my current hair'. -랑 links the comparison reference ('current hair'); 비슷하게 is the adverb of 비슷하다 ('to be similar'). The phrase is the standard request for maintenance with minor adjustments allowed.
존댓말 to staff. Used by returning clients who already have a style they like and just want it maintained. -랑 is colloquial; fine in the salon chair. 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 is the returning-customer variant.

비슷하게 = similar (minor tweaks OK) / 똑같이 = identical (exact copy) / 그대로 = as-is (no change). Choose 비슷하게 when small adjustments are welcome; 똑같이 when you need a precise repeat; 그대로 when you want zero change in style.
크게 바꾸지 말고 비슷하게 해 주세요 (stacking 'no big changes'); 지금 머리랑 비슷하게, 길이만 좀 줄여 주세요 (style same, length tweaked); 지난번에 해 주신 거랑 비슷하게 (reference a past visit).
Two traps: (1) 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게 — redundant; 처럼 and 비슷하게 overlap; use one frame only; (2) 지금 머리 같게 — 같다 as an adverb this way sounds unnatural; use 비슷하게 or 똑같이 instead.

mistakes: Mixing 처럼 and 비슷하게 as 지금 머리처럼 비슷하게.
처럼 already means 'like', so it's redundant with 비슷하게. Use one frame: 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요 or 지금 머리처럼 해 주세요.
Saying 지금 머리 같게 해 주세요.
같다 ('to be the same') as an adverb here sounds off. Natural is 비슷하게 ('similarly') or 똑같이 ('identically'): 지금 머리랑 비슷하게 해 주세요.
Confusing 비슷하게 (similar) with 똑같이 (identical).
비슷하게 allows minor tweaks; 똑같이 demands an exact copy. If you want it precisely the same, say 똑같이; for 'roughly the same', say 비슷하게.

usage: Polite; asking for a layered cut for movement and lightness
많이 ('a lot') for heavy, dramatic layering
The opposite: one-length, blunt cut, no stepped layers
examples: 답답해 보여서 층 좀 내 주세요.
It looks heavy, so please add some layers.
답답하다 here means 'heavy and stuffy-looking' (too much bulk with no movement) — a natural reason to request 층
층 내 주시고, 숱도 좀 쳐 주세요.
Layers please, and thin it out a bit too.
Pairing 층 내다 (layers for movement) with 숱 치다 (thinning for density) — related but distinct services
A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 층 너무 많이 내지 말고 자연스럽게 해 주세요.
A: How would you like it? / B: Don't over-layer — keep it natural.
층 너무 많이 내지 말고 ('without over-layering') + 자연스럽게 ('naturally') steers the stylist away from heavy steps
nuance: 층 내 주세요 is 층 ('layer', Sino-Korean 層 — the same character as a building floor) + 내다 ('to produce, bring out') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. The essential collocation is 층(을) 내다 = 'to create a layered cut'; the verb is specifically 내다 (transitive: you bring them out), while 층이 나다 is the intransitive form ('layers appear/form'). Knowing this transitive/intransitive pair explains the opposite: 층 안 나게 해 주세요 uses 나다 ('don't let layers form'). A closely related but different service is 숱 치기 ('thinning', reducing density): 층 내다 creates stepped lengths for movement and volume, while 숱 치다 reduces bulk without necessarily changing the length steps — English speakers often conflate these as 'layering', but they are separate requests to the stylist. The loanword 레이어 exists on some salon menus, but plain 층 is what Koreans actually say in the chair. The idiom pair 내다/나다 is important: 층을 내다 (stylist makes layers) vs. 층이 나다 (layers result/appear) — get the transitivity right.

structuredNuance.t: 층 (Sino-Korean 層, 'layer/floor') + 내다 ('to bring out/produce') + 주세요. The fixed collocation is 층(을) 내다 = cut layers into the hair. The result is stepped lengths that add movement and reduce visual weight. Opposite: 층 안 나게 해 주세요 (one-length, no layers).
존댓말 to the stylist. Said during the style consultation, often paired with 숱 치기 requests. 좀 softens the request: 층 좀 내 주세요 ('a bit of layering, please').

층 내다 = create stepped lengths for movement; 숱 치다 = reduce thickness/density with thinning shears. You can have one without the other. Many English speakers ask for 'layers' wanting only thinning — clarify which you actually need.
층 is Sino-Korean 層, the same word as a building floor (1층 = first floor, 2층 = second floor). In hair it means a 'stepped level' — the same structural idea.

Two traps: (1) saying 층을 만들어 주세요 — understandable but unidiomatic; the natural verb is 내다, not 만들다; (2) confusing layering (층 내다) with thinning (숱 치다) — they are different services and require different tools.

mistakes: Saying 층 만들어 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for layering is 내다, not 만들다: 층 내 주세요. 만들다 ('make') sounds off with 층.
Confusing 층 내기 (layers) with 숱 치기 (thinning).
층 내다 creates stepped lengths for movement; 숱 치다 reduces thickness/density. They're different — say what you actually want.
Pronouncing/writing it as 칭 or mixing with 청.
It's 층 (cheung, 'layer/floor'). Don't confuse it with similar-sounding syllables; the request is 층 내 주세요.

english: Please thin it out a bit
usage: Please thin it out a bit
Polite; reduce hair density/bulk with thinning shears
많이 for heavier, more aggressive thinning
When you want to keep all the volume
examples: 머리숱이 너무 많아서 숱 좀 쳐 주세요.
My hair's too thick, so please thin it out.
머리숱이 많다 ('to have dense/thick hair') is the natural way to describe having lots of hair — the reason for the request
윗부분은 두고 아래쪽만 숱 쳐 주세요.
Leave the top, just thin out underneath.
Zone-targeting: 아래쪽만 ('only the bottom part') keeps the crown full while reducing bulk below
A: 숱 많이 쳐 드릴까요? / B: 숱 너무 많이는 치지 마시고 조금만요.
A: Shall I thin it out a lot? / B: Don't thin it too much — just a little.
조금만 ('just a little') caps the thinning and is a good response to prevent over-thinning
nuance: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요 is 숱 ('the density/amount of one's hair') + 좀 (softener) + 치다 ('to strike', here used as the set verb 'to thin out') in the -아/어 주세요 favor form. The key vocabulary is 숱 itself: 머리숱이 많다 means 'to have dense/thick hair', while 숱이 적다 means 'sparse/thin hair'. This is about DENSITY (how many hairs there are per square centimetre), not about the length or the individual strand width. The fixed collocation is 숱(을) 치다 — the stylists uses thinning shears to remove bulk without dramatically shortening the hair. Crucially, 층 내다 (layering for movement) and 숱 치다 (thinning for density) are different services; you can layer without thinning and vice versa. The English-speaker trap is conflating 'thin out' with 얇게 하다: 얇다 describes how THIN each individual strand is (strand width), not how dense the overall hair is — saying 머리 얇게 해 주세요 is a category error. The verb 치다 has many unrelated meanings (hit, play, count), so learners doubt it, but 숱 치다 is completely standard salon Korean. Also note the vowel: 숱 (su-l), not 술 (su-l for alcohol) — one consonant change makes a very different word.

structuredNuance.t: 숱 ('hair density/amount') + 치다 ('to thin out', set verb) + 주세요. The collocation 숱(을) 치다 means removing bulk with thinning shears — reducing HOW MANY hairs there are per area, without dramatically changing length or strand width.
존댓말 to the stylist. Used by anyone with naturally thick, heavy hair who wants it to sit lighter. 좀 softens the request politely. Stack 윗부분은 두고 / 아래쪽만 to target a specific zone.

숱 치다 = thin by reducing density; 층 내다 = thin by creating stepped lengths for movement. These are physically different techniques. Many English speakers mean 숱 치기 when they say 'layers' — check which you actually want.
숱 많이 쳐 주세요 (aggressive thinning); 숱 치지 말아 주세요 (keep the volume); 아래쪽만 숱 쳐 주세요 (zone-targeted thinning).

Two traps: (1) 머리 얇게 해 주세요 — 얇다 is about strand width, not density; use 숱(을) 치다 for bulk reduction; (2) doubting the verb 치다 because it usually means 'hit' — 숱 치다 is the fully standard, idiomatic salon phrase for thinning.

mistakes: Saying 머리 얇게 해 주세요 to mean 'thin it out'.
얇다 is about the width of each strand, not density. To reduce bulk, say 숱(을) 쳐 주세요 ('thin out the volume').
Using a different verb like 숱 줄여 주세요.
The idiomatic collocation is 숱(을) 치다. 줄이다 ('reduce') is understandable but unnatural here; say 숱 좀 쳐 주세요.
Confusing 숱 with 술.
숱 = hair density; 술 = alcohol. Keep the ㅌ: 숱 좀 쳐 주세요, not 술 좀 쳐 주세요.

english: Please make the sides and back short
usage: Make the sides and back short
Polite; the backbone instruction for a classic short men's cut
반말, to a friend cutting your hair
The natural pairing: 윗머리 ('top hair') kept longer
Just clean up the sides and back
정리하다 ('tidy up') for a lighter maintenance cleanup, not a full cut
examples: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 하고, 윗머리는 그대로 두세요.
Sides and back short, leave the top as is.
The standard two-instruction combo: short zones explicitly named, top left untouched with 두다 ('leave')
옆이랑 뒤는 짧게, 투블럭으로 해 주세요.
Sides and back short — give me a two-block.
투블럭 (the undercut/two-block style) is the default men's style name in Korean barbershops; naming it cuts the consultation time
A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 옆은 귀 보이게, 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요.
A: How would you like it? / B: Sides so the ears show, back short.
귀 보이게 ('so ears show') is the most concrete, universally understood length cue for the sides
nuance: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요 is 옆 ('side') + -이랑 (colloquial 'and', after consonant) + 뒤 ('back') + 는 (topic marker) + 짧게 (adverb 'short') + 해 주세요. This single instruction frames a typical short men's haircut by naming the zones: 옆 (sides), 뒤 (back), 윗머리 (top), 앞머리 (front/bangs). Memorising these four zone words gives you full directional control at any barbershop. The particle -이랑 after a consonant (and -랑 after a vowel) is the spoken equivalent of -과/와. The topic marker 는 on 뒤는 sets up a contrast — 'as for the sides and back…' — leaving the top implicitly as the contrasting zone. In Korean barbershops the style name 투블럭 (two-block undercut: very short sides, longer top) covers the most common variant and can replace the whole description once you know the term. The English-speaker trap is adjective form: 짧게 (adverb, used before 해 주세요) vs. 짧은 (noun-modifier — you can't say 짧은 해 주세요). Also, 옆 (side) and 앞 (front) are easy to confuse when stressed; make sure you mean 옆 (sides of the head) rather than 앞 (front).

structuredNuance.t: 옆 ('side') + -이랑 ('and') + 뒤 ('back') + 는 (topic marker) + 짧게 (adverb of 짧다 'short') + 해 주세요. Zone-based instruction: name the head sections you want short, implicitly contrasting with the top which is left longer.
존댓말 to any barber or stylist. Primarily a men's cut instruction. Pair immediately with 윗머리는 길게 / 그대로 to complete the picture. Saying 투블럭으로 해 주세요 achieves the same result with a single style name.

투블럭으로 해 주세요 = name the style directly (shorter sides, longer top with a visible line of difference). 옆이랑 뒤만 정리해 주세요 = just clean up those zones, less dramatic. 짧게 vs. 정리 signals the degree of shortening.
옆은 귀 보이게 해 주세요 (sides: ears visible); 뒤는 목선 정리해 주세요 (back: clean up the neckline); 투블럭으로 짧게 해 주세요 (two-block style, explicitly short).

Two traps: (1) 짧은 해 주세요 — wrong form; before 해 주세요 you need the adverb 짧게, not the modifier 짧은; (2) confusing 옆 (side) with 앞 (front) — these are different zones, and mixing them produces the wrong cut.

mistakes: Saying 짧은 해 주세요.
Before 해 주세요 you need the adverb 짧게, not the modifier 짧은. Correct: 짧게 해 주세요.
Mixing up 옆 (side) and 앞 (front).
옆 = the sides of the head; 앞 = the front. For a typical cut you shorten 옆이랑 뒤 (sides and back); don't accidentally say 앞.
Forgetting the topic marker, blurting 옆 뒤 짧게.
It's understandable but choppy. The natural phrasing groups them: 옆이랑 뒤는 짧게 해 주세요.

english: Please wash my hair / give me a shampoo
usage: Polite; asking staff to shampoo you — requires the causative form
반말, to a friend or family member
Fuller form with 머리 spelled out — clearer if context is ambiguous
Is it okay if I don't wash it (myself)?
Asking whether you need to arrive with clean hair or if they will wash it
examples: 커트 전에 머리 감겨 주세요.
Please shampoo my hair before the cut.
커트 전에 ('before the cut') pins the timing — many salons wash first, but it's worth confirming
염색했으니까 깨끗하게 감겨 주세요.
I got it dyed, so please wash it clean.
깨끗하게 ('cleanly') after a dye signals you want a thorough rinse, not a quick splash
A: 물 온도 괜찮으세요? / B: 네, 감겨 주세요.
A: Is the water temperature okay? / B: Yes, please go ahead and wash it.
Standard exchange at the shampoo basin; 네 confirms the temperature, then 감겨 주세요 gives the go-ahead
nuance: 감겨 주세요 is the CAUSATIVE of 감다 ('to wash one's own hair'): 감다 → 감기다 ('to wash someone else's hair') → 감겨 주다 ('to wash someone's hair for them as a favor'). This causative shift is the central grammar point and the #1 learner trap. When YOU wash your own hair at home, the verb is 머리(를) 감다. At the salon, the staff wash YOUR hair, so the customer uses the causative 감기다 → 감겨 주세요 ('please have my hair washed / please wash my hair for me'). Saying 머리 감아 주세요 (plain 감다 + 주세요) is a common learner error that technically sounds like you're asking the stylist to wash their own hair as a favor — Koreans understand from context, but 감겨 주세요 is the correct causative. Compare: 머리 감았어요 ('I washed my hair', plain, about yourself) vs. 머리 감겨 주세요 ('please wash my hair', causative, you want the staff to do it). Also note: 감다 is specific to HAIR; for face-washing use 세수하다, for body-washing use 씻다 — don't generalise 감다 to any body-washing context.

structuredNuance.t: 감겨 주세요 is the causative of 감다: 감다 ('wash own hair') → 감기다 ('wash someone else's hair') → 감겨 주세요 ('please wash [my hair] for me'). The causative form is the grammatically correct form when you are the one being washed, not doing the washing.
존댓말 to salon staff at the shampoo basin. 감다 is specific to hair-washing; do not use it for face (세수하다) or body (씻다). 머리 감겨 주세요 is the clearer version if context is at all ambiguous.
감아 주세요 (plain stem + favor) is a common learner error — technically asks the stylist to wash their own hair as a favor. Only 감겨 주세요 (causative) is correct when asking the staff to wash yours.
머리 감겨 주세요 (with 머리 for clarity); 깨끗하게 감겨 주세요 (wash it cleanly/thoroughly); 커트 전에 감겨 주세요 (before the cut). The 반말 form is 감겨 줘.

English uses 'wash' regardless of who does it, so the 감다/감기다 distinction is invisible. This is the single most common grammar error at the salon: learners say 감아 주세요 instead of the correct causative 감겨 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 머리 감아 주세요 to the stylist.
감다 is washing your OWN hair. To ask staff to wash yours, use the causative 감기다: 감겨 주세요 ('wash my hair for me').
Using 씻겨 주세요 for hair.
씻다/씻기다 is for washing the body or objects. Hair specifically takes 감다/감기다: 머리 감겨 주세요.
Confusing 감다 (wash hair) with 감다 (close eyes / wind).
감다 is a homonym (also 'close the eyes', 'wind up'). In the salon it means washing hair; context and 머리 make it clear: 머리 감겨 주세요.

english: Please blow-dry and style it too
usage: Polite; include drying and styling as the finishing step
You don't need to blow-dry it
Declining the dry/style — usually fine for casual visits
Can I get just a blow-out today?
Asking for styling only, no cut — 드라이 as a standalone service
examples: 오늘 약속 있어서 드라이까지 해 주세요.
I have plans today, so please style it too.
약속 있다 ('have plans') is the social reason Koreans give for requesting the full styled finish — the stylist understands immediately
커트하고 드라이까지 해 주세요. 얼마예요?
A cut and a blow-out too, please — how much?
Bundle both services in one sentence and immediately check the combined price — common in Korean salons where 드라이 may cost extra
A: 드라이해 드릴까요? / B: 네, 안쪽으로 살짝 말리게 드라이해 주세요.
A: Shall I blow-dry it? / B: Yes — please blow-dry it curling slightly inward.
안쪽으로 말리게 ('curling inward') directs the style direction; 바깥쪽으로 would be outward curling
nuance: 드라이까지 해 주세요 is 드라이 (loanword 'dry', meaning a professional blow-dry and styling) + -까지 ('even, up to and including') + 해 주세요. The particle -까지 carries the meaning 'go all the way through to the styling step as well' — it implies the cut is assumed and you want the process completed with a full finish. In Korean salons 드라이 is a professionally blown-out and styled finish, often using a round brush and a blow-dryer; it is sometimes a paid add-on on the menu, not simply towel-drying. The English-speaker trap is interpreting 드라이 as 'dry' in the basic sense: it means a full styled blow-out, so don't be surprised if it costs extra or needs to be listed on the service ticket. The particle nuance matters: -까지 ('up to / including') emphasises completion of the process, whereas -도 ('also') in 드라이도 해 주세요 simply adds it as another item — both work, but -까지 sounds more like 'finish it off properly'. Treat 드라이 as a 하다-noun: 드라이를 하다 / 드라이해 주세요. To decline, say 드라이 안 해도 돼요 — perfectly natural.

structuredNuance.t: 드라이 (loanword, a professional blow-dry and styled finish) + -까지 ('up to and including') + 해 주세요. -까지 signals 'complete the service all the way through to the styling step'. In Korean salons this is a full blow-out with a brush, not just removing water.
존댓말 to staff. Said at the end of the consultation or when you want to confirm the full service. If you're just going home with no plans, 드라이 안 해도 돼요 is a fine, polite decline.

드라이도 해 주세요 ('do the blow-dry too') adds it as one more item in a list; 드라이까지 해 주세요 emphasises completing the whole process through to styling. Both are correct — -까지 is more emphatic about finishing properly.
드라이만 받을 수 있어요? (blow-out only, no cut); 안쪽으로 말리게 드라이해 주세요 (inward curl); 바깥쪽으로 드라이해 주세요 (outward/volume). 드라이 takes 하다: 드라이해 주세요.

Two traps: (1) 드라이 = 'dry' in English, so learners assume it is included automatically — in Korean salons it is often a paid add-on; always confirm with 드라이까지 해 주세요 or check the menu; (2) misplacing 만 — 드라이 해 주세요만 puts 만 at the sentence end (wrong); 만 must attach to the noun: 드라이만 해 주세요 ('only a blow-out, nothing else').

mistakes: Thinking 드라이 just means 'dry it off'.
In Korean salons 드라이 means a styled blow-out (often a paid service), not merely removing water. It may be an extra menu item.
Saying 드라이 해 주세요만 with 만 at the end.
만 attaches to the noun: 드라이만 해 주세요 ('only a blow-out'). Tacked onto the sentence end it's broken.
Confusing -까지 ('including') with -부터 ('from/starting').
-까지 means 'up to/including' the blow-dry. -부터 ('from') would wrongly mean 'starting from the blow-dry'. Use 드라이까지.

english: I'd like to get a perm
usage: I'd like to get a perm
Polite; opening that you want a perm — the -는데요 invites the stylist's guidance
I came to get a perm
States your purpose for the visit rather than just your desire
Asking the stylist to suggest the right style for your hair
examples: 오늘 펌하고 싶은데요. 시간 얼마나 걸려요?
I'd like a perm today — how long does it take?
Perms take two to three hours; asking 시간 얼마나 걸려요 immediately after is essential before committing
자연스러운 펌하고 싶은데, 어떤 게 좋을까요?
I want a natural perm — which would be good?
자연스러운 ('natural') narrows the style, then 어떤 게 좋을까요 ('which is good?') hands the choice to the expert
A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 손상 안 되게 펌하고 싶은데요. 추천해 주시겠어요?
A: What can I do for you? / B: I'd like a perm without too much damage — could you recommend one?
손상 안 되게 ('without causing damage') + 추천해 주시겠어요? is the polished consultation opener for first-time perm customers
nuance: 펌하고 싶은데요 is 펌 (loanword 'perm', from 'permanent wave') + 하고 싶다 ('want to do') + the soft ender -는데요. The word choice matters: younger salon Korean firmly prefers 펌, while 파마 is the older colloquial form still understood but increasingly dated. The -는데요 ender softens and extends an implicit question ('I want a perm, so… what do you recommend?'), making the phrase a natural consultation opener rather than a flat statement. Contrast with 펌하려고 왔어요 ('I came to get a perm') which declares purpose; both are natural openers, but 싶은데요 signals you're open to the stylist's input, while 하려고 왔어요 sounds more decided. Because Korean perm culture has many styles — 셋팅펌 (setting perm), 열펌 (digital/hot perm), 볼륨매직 (volume magic), 스트레이트 펌 (straight perm) — the stylist will almost always ask which type; proactively saying 자연스러운 펌 or 추천 좀 해 주세요 saves a back-and-forth. The English-speaker trap is the want-construction: 하고 싶어요 alone is fine but can sound blunt as an opener; -는데요 turns it into a softer, more conversational lead-in.

structuredNuance.t: 펌 (loanword 'perm') + 하고 싶다 ('want to do') + -는데요 (soft ender). The -는데요 means 'I want a perm, so…' — trailing off and inviting the stylist's response. It's a consultation opener, not a command or a simple statement.
존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the start of the appointment. Because a perm is a long, costly service, always follow up with 시간 얼마나 걸려요? and 가격이 어떻게 돼요? before the stylist starts.
펌하고 싶은데요 ('I'd like a perm, what do you think?') — open, invites advice. 펌하려고 왔는데요 ('I came to get a perm') — states purpose, slightly more decided. 파마 exists but is dated; use 펌.
자연스러운 펌하고 싶은데요 ('a natural perm'); 셋팅펌 / 열펌 / 볼륨매직 하고 싶은데요 (naming the style); 손상 안 되게 펌하고 싶은데요 ('a perm with minimal damage').

The trap is the want-construction register: 펌하고 싶어요 alone is grammatically fine but can sound blunt as an opener. Pairing with -는데요 makes it conversational and invites input — the natural Korean way to begin a consultation.

mistakes: Saying 펌 주세요 like ordering a product.
A perm is a service you 'do', not 'receive' like an object. Use 펌하고 싶은데요 or 펌하려고요, not 펌 주세요.
Defaulting to 파마 thinking it's the only word.
파마 is older/colloquial; current salon Korean prefers 펌. Both are understood, but 펌하고 싶은데요 sounds more natural now.
Dropping -는데요 to a blunt 펌하고 싶어요 and stopping.
It's fine but abrupt as a conversation opener. -는데요 invites the stylist's input: 펌하고 싶은데요 (어떤 게 좋을까요?).

english: I'd like to dye my hair — could you suggest a color?
usage: I want to dye it — please suggest a color
Polite; a full consultation opener combining desire + request for advice
I wanna dye it — what color's good?
I just want a root touch-up
뿌리 염색 ('root dye') for covering regrowth only
Do I need to bleach it (first)?
Asking whether bleaching is required before the desired color
examples: 염색하고 싶은데 너무 튀지 않는 색으로 추천해 주세요.
I'd like to dye it — suggest a color that's not too flashy.
너무 튀지 않는 ('not too flashy') guides the palette before the stylist opens the swatch book
염색하고 싶은데, 제 피부톤에 뭐가 어울려요?
I want to dye it — what suits my skin tone?
피부톤에 어울리다 ('suit the skin tone') asks for a personalised recommendation, not just a popular color
A: 오늘 뭐 해 드릴까요? / B: 흰머리 가리게 염색하고 싶은데 추천해 주세요.
A: What would you like today? / B: I'd like to dye to cover the gray — any suggestions?
흰머리 가리다 ('cover gray hair') is one of the most common dyeing motivations in Korean salons
nuance: 염색하고 싶은데 색 추천해 주세요 chains 염색(을) 하다 ('to dye hair', Sino-Korean 染色 'dye-color') + 하고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데 (connector, 'and so') + 색 ('color') + 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend'). The connector -는데 bridges the wish and the request in a single, natural utterance rather than two choppy sentences. Essential vocabulary: 염색 = coloring/dyeing; 뿌리 염색 = root touch-up (just the regrowth near the scalp); 탈색 = bleaching (stripping pigment, often needed before vivid or light colors); 새치/흰머리 염색 = covering gray. The English-speaker trap is over-relying on the loanword 컬러: 컬러 appears on salon menus but the verb for the act is 염색하다, so 'I want to color my hair' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요. A second trap is the grammar of 추천: 추천 is a 하다-noun and cannot stand alone as a command or object of 주다 — it needs 하다: 색 추천해 주세요, never 색을 추천 주세요. Also keep 염색 (adding color) and 탈색 (removing color/bleaching) clearly distinct — many vivid or light shades require 탈색 first, which takes extra time and causes additional damage.

structuredNuance.t: 염색(을) 하다 (Sino-Korean 染色, 'dye-color') + 하고 싶다 ('want to') + -는데 (connector) + 색 ('color') + 추천해 주세요. The -는데 links desire to request in one breath — natural Korean consultation language. The full phrase says: 'I want to dye it, and so please recommend a color'.

존댓말 to the stylist. Said at the very start of the consultation. Because color choice depends on skin tone, hair condition, and lifestyle, this opener immediately cues the stylist to ask clarifying questions before reaching for the swatch book.
염색 (dye/add color) vs. 탈색 (bleach/remove color) — these are opposite processes. Requesting a light or vivid color may prompt 탈색해야 돼요? ('do we need to bleach?'). Know which you want before you ask.
염색 is Sino-Korean 染色: 染 = 'dye/stain', 色 = 'color'. The same 染 appears in 탈색 (脫色: strip-color = bleach) and 새치 염색 (covering gray hair).
Two traps: (1) 컬러하고 싶어요 — 컬러 is a menu noun, not a verb; use 염색하고 싶어요; (2) 색 추천 주세요 — 추천 is a 하다-noun; you must say 추천해 주세요, never 추천 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 컬러하고 싶어요 for 'dye my hair'.
The verb is 염색하다. 컬러 is a noun in menus, but 'I want to dye it' is 염색하고 싶어요, not 컬러하고 싶어요.
Saying 색 추천 주세요 without 하다.
추천 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. It needs 하다: 색 추천해 주세요.
Confusing 염색 (dye) with 탈색 (bleach).
염색 adds color; 탈색 strips it to lighten. For a bright shade you may need 탈색 first — ask 탈색해야 돼요?, not just 염색해 주세요.

english: Please dye it back to my natural color
usage: Make it my original hair color
Polite; returning to your natural shade after dyeing or bleaching
When you don't know your exact natural shade, naming a close natural tone
Capping brightness when you want a darker, more natural result
examples: 탈색했던 거 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.
I had it bleached — please put it back to my natural color.
탈색했던 거 ('the bleached part') tells the stylist the history so they know the starting condition
취업 때문에 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.
For job-hunting, please dye it back to natural.
취업 때문에 ('for getting a job') is one of the most common stated reasons in Korean salons — many workplaces expect dark, natural-looking hair
A: 어떤 색으로 해 드릴까요? / B: 원래 머리색이랑 비슷하게, 좀 어둡게 해 주세요.
A: What color would you like? / B: Similar to my natural color, a bit darker please.
비슷하게 + 어둡게 ('similar to natural, but slightly darker') fine-tunes the shade and gives the stylist a clear target
nuance: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요 is 원래 ('original, originally', Sino-Korean 元來) + 머리색 ('hair color') + -으로 ('to/into', the result/direction particle) + 해 주세요. The critical grammar is -(으)로: this particle marks what something is changed INTO — 'make it INTO my original color'. The pattern 'X(으)로 해 주세요' = 'please make it X' is reusable for any target color: 어두운 갈색으로 해 주세요 ('make it dark brown'), 검은색으로 해 주세요 ('make it black'). After the consonant ㄱ in 색, the particle form is 색으로 (not 색로). 원래 means 'as it originally was / in its natural state'; it's extremely common in Korea where students and office workers often darken their hair back to a natural shade for 취업 (job hunting) or school rules. The English-speaker trap is the particle: learners use 원래 머리색을 해 주세요 (object particle 을) or 머리색에 해 주세요 (locative 에), but the change-into meaning needs -(으)로. Also distinguish 원래 ('originally') from 원해 ('want', from 원하다) — one letter apart but completely different.

structuredNuance.t: 원래 ('original, originally', Sino-Korean 元來) + 머리색 ('hair color') + -으로 ('into/to', change-result particle) + 해 주세요. The phrase means 'please transform the color back into my original natural shade'. -(으)로 is what makes this a change-into request, not just a description.
존댓말 to the stylist. Common at the start of a job-hunting season (취업준비), before school term, or simply when a customer is done with dyed hair. Pair with 좀 어둡게 or 자연스럽게 to add precision.

검은색으로 해 주세요 ('make it black') forces pure black, which can look unnatural on non-Asian natural hair; 원래 머리색으로 targets the personal natural shade, which is usually a very dark brown (흑갈색). These are different results.
원래 is Sino-Korean 元來: 元 = 'original/root', 來 = 'come/from'. It means 'as it originally came' — a natural fit for 'my original hair color'.
The particle trap: learners say 원래 머리색을 해 주세요 (을 = object) or 머리색에 해 주세요 (에 = locative), but the change-into meaning needs -(으)로. After the ㄱ in 색, the correct form is 색으로: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요.

mistakes: Using 을/를 instead of (으)로: 원래 머리색을 해 주세요.
The 'change it INTO' meaning needs the particle -(으)로: 원래 머리색으로 해 주세요. -을/를 marks an object, not a result.
Confusing 원래 ('originally') with 원해 ('want').
원래 머리색 = 'original hair color'. 원해 is from 원하다 ('to want'). Don't write 원해 머리색.
Saying 검은색으로 when you mean your natural shade.
Natural hair may be dark brown, not pure black. For your real shade say 원래 머리색으로; 검은색 ('black') forces full black, which can look unnatural.

usage: Polite-neutral; direct way to ask a service's price
How much would a cut be?
Softer/more polite with -인가요, used with unfamiliar or upscale staff
-부터 ('starting from') asks for the bottom of a price range
examples: 남자 커트 얼마예요?
How much is a men's cut?
남자/여자 커트 are often priced differently; always specify gender to get the right quote
커트하고 염색하면 다 해서 얼마예요?
A cut and dye — how much all together?
다 해서 ('all together') asks for the combined total of multiple services
A: 어서 오세요. / B: 학생 할인 돼요? 커트 얼마예요?
A: Welcome! / B: Is there a student discount? How much is a cut?
학생 할인 ('student discount') is genuinely worth asking about in Korean salons — many offer one
nuance: 커트 얼마예요? is 커트 ('a haircut') + 얼마 ('how much in price') + 예요 (polite copula), the simplest and most direct way to ask a service's cost. The word 얼마 specifically asks about PRICE; it is not to be confused with 얼마나 ('how much/long', about extent or duration). This is the most common learner mix-up at the salon: 얼마예요? = 'how much does it cost?', while 얼마나 걸려요? = 'how long does it take?' — one extra syllable but completely different questions. Korean salons frequently price differently by gender (남자/여자 커트) and by hair length, so specifying 남자 커트 or 긴 머리 커트 before 얼마예요 gets you an accurate answer. Add-ons like perms and dye are always billed separately, so asking 다 해서 얼마예요? after listing services is standard practice. The English-speaker trap is the copula: 얼마 + 예요 fuses naturally (얼마예요), not the separated 얼마 이에요. Bare 커트 얼마예요? is more natural than the heavier 커트 가격이 얼마예요? ('what is the price of a haircut?') — the word 가격 is usually unnecessary.

structuredNuance.t: 커트 ('haircut') + 얼마 ('how much in price') + 예요 (polite copula). 얼마 is the Korean word specifically for a price/amount of money. It fuses directly with the copula: 얼마예요, not 얼마 이에요.
Polite-neutral; fine with any staff. Ask before sitting down to avoid surprises. Specify 남자/여자, 긴 머리/짧은 머리 for an accurate quote, as salons routinely price by gender and hair length.

얼마예요? = cost (price question). 얼마나 걸려요? = duration (time question). One extra syllable separates them, but they are completely different questions — never swap them. 얼마부터예요? asks for the starting price of a range.
남자 커트 얼마예요? (men's cut price); 다 해서 얼마예요? (combined total); 펌은 얼마부터예요? (perm starting price); 학생 할인 되나요? (student discount).
Two traps: (1) 얼마 vs. 얼마나 — 얼마예요 asks price; 얼마나 걸려요 asks duration; these are completely different; (2) over-building as 커트 가격이 얼마예요? — understandable but heavy; natives say 커트 얼마예요?.

mistakes: Confusing 얼마 (price) with 얼마나 (extent/duration).
얼마예요? asks the cost; 얼마나 걸려요? asks the time. To ask price, use 얼마: 커트 얼마예요?.
Saying 얼마 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses after a vowel: 얼마 + 예요 → 얼마예요. Writing 얼마 이에요 is unnatural; say 커트 얼마예요?.
Over-building it as 커트 가격이 얼마예요?
It's correct but heavy. Natives simply say 커트 얼마예요?; the word 가격 ('price') is usually unnecessary.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking the duration of a service
About how long might it take?
Softer with 시간 + -ㄹ까요, implying 'I'm just wondering'
Quick yes/no version with 오래 ('a long time')
examples: 펌하면 얼마나 걸려요?
If I get a perm, how long does it take?
펌하면 ('if perming') ties the duration question to the specific service — essential since perms run two to three hours
뒤에 약속이 있어서요. 얼마나 걸려요?
I have an appointment after — how long will it take?
뒤에 약속 ('plans after') is the natural reason Koreans give when they need to time-budget their salon visit
A: 염색까지 하면 시간 얼마나 걸릴까요? / B: 두 시간 정도 걸려요.
A: Including the dye, about how long? / B: About two hours.
염색까지 하면 ('if including dye') shows how to stack multiple services into one duration question
nuance: 얼마나 걸려요? is 얼마나 ('how much, to what extent') + 걸리다 ('to take time, to require') in polite question form. The verb 걸리다 is the standard Korean for 'time is taken' — it is intransitive, meaning time functions as the SUBJECT: 한 시간 걸려요 = '(it) takes an hour', literally 'one hour is required'. This is the opposite of English 'it takes an hour', where 'it' is subject and 'an hour' is object. The key distinction is 얼마나 걸려요 (duration, extent) vs. 얼마예요 (price) — identical opening syllables but completely different questions. The English-speaker trap with the verb is twofold: (1) treating 시간 as the object and saying 시간을 얼마나 걸려요? — wrong because 걸리다 is intransitive; use 시간(이) 얼마나 걸려요? or simply 얼마나 걸려요?; (2) confusing 걸리다 with 걷다 ('to walk') or 걸다 ('to hang/call'), which are different verbs entirely. Adding 시간 upfront and softening with -ㄹ까요 (시간 얼마나 걸릴까요?) makes the question more tentative and polite for a service context.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마나 ('how much/how greatly') + 걸리다 ('to take time, be required') in a polite question. 걸리다 is intransitive — time is the subject: 한 시간 걸려요 ('one hour is taken'). Asking this is essential before any long service like a perm or dye.

Polite-neutral; used with any staff. Said right after naming the service you want, especially for perms (2–3 hours), full dye jobs (1–2 hours), or complex cuts. If you have plans afterwards, state 뒤에 약속이 있어서요 as context.
얼마나 걸려요 = duration (how much time). 얼마예요 = price (how much money). These look similar but ask completely different things. Use 얼마나 for time, 얼마 for cost — never swap.
시간 얼마나 걸릴까요? (softer, 'I wonder how long'); 오래 걸려요? (quick binary: long or not?); 펌하면 얼마나 걸려요? (tied to a specific service).

Two traps: (1) 시간을 얼마나 걸려요? — 걸리다 is intransitive; 시간 takes the subject particle 이/가, not the object particle 을/를; (2) confusing 걸리다 ('take time') with 걸다 ('hang / make a call') — they share a similar form but are different verbs.

mistakes: Marking 시간 as object: 시간을 얼마나 걸려요?
걸리다 is intransitive; time is the subject, not the object. Say 시간(이) 얼마나 걸려요? or simply 얼마나 걸려요?.
Using 걸어요 instead of 걸려요.
걸다 ('hang / make a phone call') is a different verb. The time-taking verb is 걸리다: 얼마나 걸려요?.
Confusing 얼마나 (how long/much-extent) with 얼마 (how much-price).
얼마예요? asks the price; 얼마나 걸려요? asks the duration. To ask time, use 얼마나, not 얼마.

hangul: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
english: I'm not happy with it — could you redo it?
usage: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
I don't like it — could you redo it?
Polite; the diplomatic, face-saving way to raise dissatisfaction and request a fix
이거 마음에 안 들어, 다시 해 줄 수 있어?
I don't like this — can you redo it?
조금만 더 다듬어 주실 수 있어요?
Could you trim it a bit more?
Softer: requesting a small adjustment rather than a full redo
여기 좀 더 짧게 해 주세요
Please make it a bit shorter here
Pinpointing a specific area that needs fixing instead of redoing everything
examples: 죄송한데, 생각했던 거랑 좀 달라서 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?
Sorry, it's a bit different from what I pictured — could you redo it?
생각했던 거랑 다르다 ('different from what I imagined') is the softest, least blaming way to state the mismatch
앞이 너무 짧은 거 같은데, 다시 봐 주실 수 있어요?
The front seems too short — could you take another look?
다시 봐 주다 ('look again') is even gentler than 다시 해 주다 ('redo') — useful when you want a reassessment, not necessarily a full fix
A: (거울 보여주며) 어떠세요? / B: 색이 생각보다 밝게 나왔는데, 조금 어둡게 다시 해 주실 수 있을까요?
A: (holding up mirror) How is it? / B: The color came out lighter than expected — could you redo it a bit darker?
Responding to the mirror check: -ㄹ 수 있을까요 makes the redo request as tentative and polite as possible
nuance: 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? combines 마음에 들다 (the fixed IDIOM 'to be to one's liking', lit. 'to enter the heart') negated as 마음에 안 들다 + -는데 (connector, 'and so') + 다시 ('again') + 해 주시다 (honorific favor verb) + -ㄹ 수 있어요? ('can you / are you able to?'). This is the standard diplomatic, face-saving formula for raising dissatisfaction in a Korean service setting — complaining outright would create awkwardness, so the -ㄹ 수 있어요? framing and the honorific -시- keep it soft and non-confrontational. The core idiom 마음에 들다 is the natural Korean verb for liking a result or outcome: 마음에 들어요 = 'I like it', 마음에 안 들어요 = 'I don't like it'. You cannot substitute 좋아하다 here — 이거 안 좋아해요 about a haircut sounds like a general dislike of haircuts as a concept, not dissatisfaction with this specific result. The English-speaker trap is exactly that substitution. The particle in the idiom is always 에 (locative): 마음에 들다 — never 마음을 들다 or 마음이 들다. Always lead with a softener (죄송한데 'sorry but'; or a reason like 생각했던 거랑 달라서 'it's different from what I imagined') before the redo request, matching Korean social norms around indirect negative feedback.

structuredNuance.t: 마음에 들다 = the idiom 'to enter the heart' = 'to be to one's liking'. Negated: 마음에 안 들다 = 'not to my liking' = 'I'm not happy with it'. This idiom is the ONLY natural way to express dissatisfaction with a service result in Korean — 좋아하다 is wrong here.
존댓말 with honorific -시- (해 주시다) and the softened ability question form -ㄹ 수 있어요?. Never a direct command (다시 하세요 is rude). Always precede with 죄송한데 or a reason to save face.

마음에 안 들어요 ('I'm not satisfied with the result') vs. 이상해요 ('it looks strange/odd') — both valid complaints, but 마음에 안 들다 is the most diplomatic. 다시 봐 주실 수 있어요? ('could you take another look?') is even softer than 다시 해 주실 수 있어요? ('could you redo it?').
조금만 더 다듬어 주실 수 있어요? (small adjustment); 여기만 조금 더 해 주실 수 있어요? (one spot); 색이 마음에 안 드는데 다시 해 주실 수 있을까요? (-ㄹ까요 for extra tentativeness).
The #1 trap: 'I don't like it' → 안 좋아해요, which is wrong for a result. Use 마음에 안 들어요. Second trap: the particle — it is always 마음에 들다 (locative 에), never 마음을 or 마음이.

mistakes: Saying 이거 안 좋아해요 to mean 'I don't like this haircut'.
좋아하다 is for general liking of people/activities. For not liking a result, use the idiom 마음에 안 들어요.
Getting the particle wrong: 마음을 안 들어요 or 마음이 안 들어요.
The idiom takes locative 에: 마음에 안 들어요 ('it doesn't enter my heart'). Not 을/를 or 이/가 on 마음.
Demanding a redo bluntly: 다시 하세요.
다시 하세요 is a command and sounds rude to staff. Ask as an ability question with honorific 시: 다시 해 주실 수 있어요?, and lead with 죄송한데.
